# Lebesgue Integral of $g(x)=x^2$ over $\mathbb{R}$

## Setup

We compute
$$\int_{\mathbb{R}} x^2\,d\lambda(x),$$
where $\lambda$ is Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb{R}$ and $g(x)=x^2\ge 0$ is measurable (continuous). For non-negative measurable functions, the Lebesgue integral is defined as the supremum of integrals of non-negative simple functions bounded above by $g$:

$$\int_{\mathbb{R}} g\,d\lambda \;=\; \sup\left\{\int_{\mathbb{R}} s\,d\lambda \;:\; 0\le s\le g,\; s\text{ simple}\right\}\;\in\;[0,+\infty].$$

Equivalently, by the monotone convergence theorem, it equals the limit of integrals over an exhausting sequence of sets.

## Exhaustion and limit

Take the exhausting sequence $A_n=[-n,n]$, so $A_n\uparrow\mathbb{R}$. Since $g\ge 0$ and $g\mathbf{1}_{A_n}\uparrow g$, the Monotone Convergence Theorem gives
$$\int_{\mathbb{R}} g\,d\lambda \;=\; \lim_{n\to\infty}\int_{[-n,n]} x^2\,d\lambda(x).$$

On each compact interval $[-n,n]$, the continuous function $x^2$ is Riemann integrable, and its Lebesgue integral agrees with the Riemann integral:
$$\int_{[-n,n]} x^2\,d\lambda(x) \;=\; \int_{-n}^{n} x^2\,dx \;=\; \left[\frac{x^3}{3}\right]_{-n}^{n} \;=\; \frac{n^3}{3}-\frac{(-n)^3}{3} \;=\; \frac{2n^3}{3}.$$

Therefore
$$\int_{\mathbb{R}} x^2\,d\lambda \;=\; \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{2n^3}{3} \;=\; +\infty.$$

## Verification of divergence (lower bound argument)

To confirm the integral is genuinely $+\infty$ (not merely that this particular exhaustion diverges), observe that for every $n\ge 1$,
$$g(x)=x^2\ge n^2\cdot\mathbf{1}_{[n,n+1]\cup[-n-1,-n]}(x),$$
so
$$\int_{\mathbb{R}} g\,d\lambda \;\ge\; n^2\cdot\lambda\big([n,n+1]\cup[-n-1,-n]\big) \;=\; n^2\cdot 2 \;=\; 2n^2.$$
Since $2n^2\to+\infty$, the integral dominates every real number, hence
$$\int_{\mathbb{R}} x^2\,d\lambda=+\infty.$$

## Conclusion

The Lebesgue integral of $g(x)=x^2$ over $\mathbb{R}$ with respect to Lebesgue measure is $+\infty$. Expressed as a limit via the exhaustion $[-n,n]\uparrow\mathbb{R}$:

$$\boxed{\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}} x^2\,d\lambda \;=\; \lim_{n\to\infty}\int_{-n}^{n}x^2\,dx \;=\; \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{2n^3}{3} \;=\; +\infty.}$$

### PROOF COMPLETE
